summary: Defines a MIB module for monitoring UDP-Lite, which is like UDP but adds partial checksum coverage. The module provides objects to describe behavior and performance of UDP-Lite endpoints. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: UDP-Lite is a version of UDP that allows damaged data to still arrive. This gives a standard set of gauges for network tools to watch it.

questions: how to monitor udp-lite with snmp
what is partial checksum coverage in udp-lite
subtitle: A standard set of SNMP counters and a table for watching UDP-Lite traffic, including partial checksum coverage.

tldr.problem: UDP-Lite resembles UDP but lets a datagram's checksum cover only part of it, so operators need a common way to monitor it and to see whether partial coverage is in use or misconfigured.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5097 defines the UDPLITE-MIB module in SMIv2, modeled on the UDP-MIB. It has datagram counters, three UDP-Lite specific counters, an endpoint table with a minimum-coverage column, and a discontinuity timestamp.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools get one portable interface for UDP-Lite statistics and can use the counters to spot bad links or wrong receiver coverage settings. The module is read-only.

today: RFC 5097 is a Proposed Standard from January 2008, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the UDPLITE-MIB module, following the pattern of the UDP-MIB in RFC 4113.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
The Lightweight User Datagram Protocol (UDP-Lite, RFC 3828) works much like UDP (RFC 768). The difference is that the UDP Length field becomes a Checksum Coverage field. That lets applications that prefer partly damaged payloads over dropped datagrams still receive them. If the feature is not used, UDP-Lite is semantically identical to UDP.

RFC 5097 defines a set of runtime statistics so that monitoring and comparison of different implementations works the same way everywhere. They are written as a MIB module in the SMIv2 format (RFC 2578). UDP-Lite has no mechanism to negotiate checksum coverage between sender and receiver; where needed, another protocol has to carry that, and DCCP (RFC 4340) is mentioned as one that can.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP-Lite is a mail service that accepts a letter even if a few words got smudged. This document says how to keep a standard set of tally marks about that mail.

sections.title: Relationship to the UDP-MIB
sections.content:
The module sits under the mib-2 subtree and follows the structure of the UDP-MIB (RFC 4113) so it is easy to integrate. It keeps the familiar counters InDatagrams, NoPorts, InErrors and OutDatagrams.

Three read-only counters are new: InPartialCov (valid received datagrams whose checksum coverage is strictly less than the datagram length), InBadChecksum (received datagrams with an invalid checksum, which also count as InErrors, unlike NoPorts) and OutPartialCov (the same idea for sent datagrams).

Two other differences from the UDP-MIB are worth knowing. All non-error counters are 64-bit, where UDP traditionally used 32-bit counters. And there is no IPv4-only listener table, because the more informative endpoint table supersedes it.
sections.plainLanguage: It copies the old UDP scoreboard and adds three new rows: how many partly covered letters came in, how many were scrambled, and how many partly covered letters went out.

sections.title: Reading the Counters
sections.content:
The RFC describes the receive path. A datagram with a valid header counts in InDatagrams. If its coverage is partial it also counts in InPartialCov, and it is delivered if the coverage is at least the receiver's minimum. Below the minimum it is discarded and, if supported, counted in EndpointViolCoverage. Header errors and checksum errors are discarded and counted in InErrors (checksum errors also in InBadChecksum), and datagrams for a port with no listener count in NoPorts.

The text suggests a simple end-to-end test. On the sender, OutPartialCov/OutDatagrams gives the fraction, between 0 and 1, of datagrams using partial coverage. On the receiver, if datagrams arrive, InErrors is close to zero and InPartialCov is zero, no partial coverage is in use. If nothing is received and InErrors grows in proportion to the sending rate, a wrong receiver minimum coverage is likely.

Some totals can be derived: incoming datagrams are InDatagrams + InErrors + NoPorts, and errors other than bad checksums are InErrors - InBadChecksum. InBadChecksum can also act as an indicator of the residual link bit error rate, so on links with higher error rates a lower coverage value may reduce both InErrors and InBadChecksum.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a mail room with bins: delivered, smudged, wrong address, and too-little-checked. By looking at which bin fills up, you can tell what is going wrong.

sections.title: The Endpoint Table
sections.content:
The udpliteEndpointTable describes each UDP-Lite endpoint where a local application is accepting or sending datagrams. It is indexed by local address type, address and port, remote address type, address and port, and an instance number used to tell apart multiple processes attached to the same endpoint (for example with the BSD socket options SO_REUSEADDR and SO_REUSEPORT).

A listener is shown in one of three ways: an application that accepts both IPv4 and IPv6 uses address type unknown(0) and a zero-length address; one that accepts only IPv4 or only IPv6 uses 0.0.0.0 or :: with the matching type; and one bound to a specific address uses that address. When the remote side is a wildcard, the remote type is unknown(0), the address is zero-length and the remote port is 0.

Beyond the index columns, udpliteEndpointProcess identifies the software tied to the endpoint, preferably using the system's native number such as sysApplElmtRunIndex or hrSWRunIndex, and zero if it cannot be identified. udpliteEndpointMinCoverage is the minimum checksum coverage the endpoint expects, where 0 means only fully covered datagrams are accepted. The optional udpliteEndpointViolCoverage counts valid datagrams dropped for being below that minimum, which separates misconfiguration from other InErrors. Index OIDs must stay within 128 sub-identifiers.

Finally, udpliteStatsDiscontinuityTime holds the sysUpTime value of the latest discontinuity in any counter, for example a loadable UDP-Lite module being loaded or unloaded. Zero means none has occurred since the management subsystem was last re-initialised.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a guest list of every mailbox in use, saying who owns it and how much of each letter they insist must be checked. A special clock notes if the counting was ever reset.

sections.title: Conformance Groups
sections.content:
The compliance statement groups the objects. Three groups are mandatory: a base group (udpliteInDatagrams, udpliteNoPorts, udpliteInErrors, udpliteOutDatagrams and udpliteStatsDiscontinuityTime), a partial checksum group (udpliteInPartialCov, udpliteInBadChecksum and udpliteOutPartialCov) and an endpoint group (udpliteEndpointProcess and udpliteEndpointMinCoverage).

The application group, which contains only udpliteEndpointViolCoverage, is optional. The RFC says it is not required to manage the transport protocol and may be implemented to help debug application design and configuration. Support for the DNS address type dns(16) is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tally boards must be kept by everyone, and one extra board is optional, for people who want to hunt down mistakes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in the module has a read-write or read-create access, so a correct implementation cannot be changed through SNMP SET operations. The readable objects can still be sensitive. The endpoint table indices, especially the local port, reveal which ports are open, which saves an attacker a port scan. udpliteEndpointMinCoverage shows what the service at a port needs, and the counters may reveal characteristics of the end-to-end path.

The RFC points out that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lack adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED to use the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and deploying older SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters can only be read, not changed. But they could tell a snoop which doors are open, so you should lock the viewing window with strong SNMP security.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: The module is registered in the SMI Numbers registry as udpliteMIB with the object identifier value { mib-2 170 }. The module itself records its revision as 18 December 2007 and credits the IETF TSV Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The module got its own official spot number, 170, in the big phone book of network management.
